Posterior predictions from an mvgam model

Source: R/predict.R
predict.mvgam.Rd

Predicts new outcomes, their expectation or the linear predictor from every posterior draw, for the training data or for new data. The section 'Which prediction function?' compares predict() with fitted.mvgam(), hindcast.mvgam() and forecast.mvgam().

Usage

# S3 method for class 'mvgam'
predict(
  object,
  newdata = NULL,
  type = c("response", "link", "expected", "variance", "terms", "latent_state",
    "detection"),
  process_error = FALSE,
  incl_autocor = FALSE,
  ndraws = NULL,
  draw_ids = NULL,
  re_formula = NULL,
  allow_new_levels = FALSE,
  sample_new_levels = "uncertainty",
  resp = NULL,
  summary = TRUE,
  robust = FALSE,
  probs = c(0.025, 0.975),
  ...
)

Arguments

object

An object of class mvgam.

newdata

Optional data frame with covariates for prediction. If NULL, uses original training data stored in the model object.

type

Character; one of "response" (default), "link", "expected", "variance", "terms", "latent_state", "detection". See Details.

process_error

Logical. FALSE, the default, leaves the trend's innovations out of the prediction. TRUE adds a random deviation at each time and series, drawn anew for every posterior draw from the spread the trend shows over the long run. For an AR(1) trend with innovation SD \(\sigma\) and coefficient \(\rho\) that spread has variance \(\sigma^2/(1-\rho^2)\). On a log link the deviations raise the average prediction by the factor \(\exp(\sigma^2/(2(1-\rho^2)))\). A random walk has no long-run spread. A ZMVN() trend has no dynamics. These two draw from the innovation covariance itself. CAR() draws from one long-run covariance at every time of an irregular grid. The argument applies under incl_autocor = FALSE. The fitted state already holds every innovation.

Each call draws new innovations. Two calls on one fit give different results. Set a seed to reproduce a result.

incl_autocor

Logical. Chooses which version of the trend each prediction uses. FALSE, the default, uses the covariate part of the model: the effects in the observation formula and the trend formula, without the trend's innovations. A prediction then depends on the covariates alone. It is the same at the first time point as at the fiftieth. Questions about covariate effects use this version. TRUE uses the fitted state, the value the trend took at each observed time as hindcast() returns it. The section 'Which prediction function?' of predict.mvgam() compares the functions.

An ELPD or an \(R^2\) describes the observed series. log_lik(), loo_R2.mvgam() and bayes_R2.mvgam() use TRUE for that reason. A time outside the training data is refused under TRUE. forecast.mvgam() predicts those times. An in-sample interval under TRUE conditions on states estimated from the same observations. It covers them more often than its nominal level. Calibration is judged out of sample, with forecast.mvgam() or lfo_cv().

The default suits a model whose covariates explain most of the signal. When most of the series-level variation lies in the trend, as in a fit with few covariates and a strong autoregressive process, the covariate part has little to say. hindcast.mvgam() and forecast.mvgam() are more informative there.

ndraws

Positive integer specifying number of posterior draws to use. NULL (default) uses all available draws.

draw_ids

Optional integer vector selecting a subset of posterior draw indices to use. NULL (default) uses all draws (subject to ndraws).

re_formula

Group-level terms to include: NULL (the default) for every one, NA for none. A formula choosing some of them is not supported.

allow_new_levels

Logical; accepted for brms compatibility. A grouping level the model never saw is refused whatever this is set to. A new level has no fitted random effect. For a new series, it has no latent state to propagate. Predict for levels the fit knows, or refit with the new levels included.

sample_new_levels

Character; accepted for brms compatibility. It has no effect, because new levels are refused. See allow_new_levels.

resp

Character specifying which response variable for multivariate models. NULL (default) returns predictions for all responses.

summary

Logical. If TRUE (the default), returns summary statistics. If FALSE, returns the full matrix of posterior draws.

robust

Logical. If FALSE (the default), uses mean and standard deviation for summaries. If TRUE, uses median and median absolute deviation (MAD).

probs

Numeric vector of probabilities for quantile computation. Default is c(0.025, 0.975) for 95% credible intervals.

...

Unused. Anything passed here is refused.

Value

With summary = FALSE, an [ndraws, nobs] matrix of draws. With summary = TRUE, a matrix with one row per observation and the columns:

  • Estimate: the posterior mean, or the median under robust = TRUE.

  • Est.Error: the posterior SD, or the MAD under robust = TRUE.

  • Q*: one quantile column per value of probs.

A multivariate model with resp = NULL gives a named list of these, one per response.

Details

type selects the quantity returned:

  • "response" (default): draws from the posterior predictive distribution on the outcome scale, from posterior_predict.mvgam().

  • "link": the linear predictor on the link scale, from posterior_linpred.mvgam().

  • "expected": the expectation E[Y | X] on the response scale, from posterior_epred.mvgam().

  • "variance": the conditional variance Var[Y | theta] per draw, from the family's mean-variance relation. It covers the gaussian, student, lognormal, poisson, bernoulli, binomial, negbinomial, gamma and beta families. Other families raise an error. By default the variance is the observation noise around the mean of the covariate part. process_error = TRUE also conditions on each draw's sampled trend innovation.

  • "terms": refused with a pointer to the functions that decompose a prediction. posterior_smooths.mvgam() returns per-smooth draws. fixef.mvgam() and ranef.mvgam() return the parametric and random-effect components.

  • "latent_state": for closure-unit families, the posterior of the latent state of each closure unit given its detection history:

    • nmix(): the latent abundance N given the observed visit counts (Royle 2004).

    • occ(): the occupancy probability P(z = 1 | y_g).

  • "detection": for nmix() and occ(), the per-visit detection probability \(p_{g,j}\) on the response scale.

Which prediction function?

Every prediction adds the latent trend to the observation model. The functions differ in the version of the trend they use and in whether they add observation noise.

FunctionTimesTrend by defaultObservation noise
fitted()training datafitted stateno
predict()anycovariate partunder type = "response"
posterior_predict()anycovariate partyes
posterior_epred(), posterior_linpred()anycovariate partno
hindcast()training datafitted stateunder type = "response"
forecast()after the training datafitted state, carried forwardunder type = "response"
residuals(), pp_check()training datafitted stateyes

The fitted state is the value the trend took at each observed time, as the model inferred it. The covariate part keeps the effects of the observation and trend formulas and leaves out the trend's innovations. Questions about covariates use it, as conditional_effects.mvgam() and the marginaleffects functions do. incl_autocor = TRUE switches predict() and the posterior_*() methods to the fitted state, the default of their brms counterparts. fitted() uses the covariate part for newdata.

References

Royle, J. A. (2004). N-mixture models for estimating population size from spatially replicated counts. Biometrics, 60, 108-115. doi:10.1111/j.0006-341X.2004.00142.x

See also

fitted.mvgam() returns expected values with the inferred trend state. forecast.mvgam() predicts future times from the fitted state. conditional_effects.mvgam() plots predictions against a covariate.

Other predictions: conditional_effects.mvgam(), conditional_smooths.mvgam(), fitted.mvgam(), hindcast.mvgam(), posterior_epred.mvgam(), posterior_linpred.mvgam(), posterior_predict.mvgam(), posterior_smooths.mvgam(), predictive_error.mvgam(), predictive_interval.mvgam()

Examples

# \dontrun{
set.seed(13)
simdat <- sim_mvgam(family = poisson(), n_series = 1L,
                     n_timepoints = 120L, trend_model = AR())
mod <- mvgam(y ~ s(x, k = 5), trend_formula = ~ AR(p = 1),
              data    = simdat$data_train,
              family  = poisson(),
              chains  = 2, silent = 2)
#> Warning: 5 of 2000 (0.0%) transitions ended with a divergence.
#> See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings for details.

# Predicted counts with their 95% intervals
head(predict(mod))
#>      Estimate Est.Error Q2.5 Q97.5
#> [1,]   2.1910  1.565166    0     6
#> [2,]  12.4240  4.268294    5    22
#> [3,]   8.3345  3.215397    3    15
#> [4,]   8.9215  3.415431    3    16
#> [5,]   4.6050  2.370186    1    10
#> [6,]   6.4860  3.172040    1    14

# The same fit on the link scale, as an expected count and as the
# variance of a count. A Poisson's variance equals its mean.
head(predict(mod, type = "link"))
#>       Estimate Est.Error      Q2.5    Q97.5
#> [1,] 0.7549232 0.2202606 0.3150363 1.175764
#> [2,] 2.5080541 0.1883211 2.1218304 2.894866
#> [3,] 2.1026189 0.1674372 1.7491777 2.425207
#> [4,] 2.1695926 0.1808300 1.8204763 2.532992
#> [5,] 1.4893140 0.2361407 1.0250207 1.938754
#> [6,] 1.8332095 0.2686246 1.3097121 2.354263
head(cbind(
  expected = predict(mod, type = "expected")[, "Estimate"],
  variance = predict(mod, type = "variance")[, "Estimate"]
))
#>       expected  variance
#> [1,]  2.179257  2.179257
#> [2,] 12.501430 12.501430
#> [3,]  8.302232  8.302232
#> [4,]  8.900367  8.900367
#> [5,]  4.558828  4.558828
#> [6,]  6.484566  6.484566

# `summary = FALSE` returns the draws, one row per draw
dim(predict(mod, summary = FALSE))
#> [1] 2000   90

# Next: forecast() predicts beyond the training times from the
# fitted trend state
# }
